title: The Morning Brief: Judge returns, SEC votes on LSU, LIV files bankruptcy
dek: Aaron Judge was activated for Tuesday's Yankees-Rockies game after three months sidelined by rib injury. The SEC escalates its LSU fight with a Thursday expulsion vote, while LIV Golf entered Chapter 11 with a BC Partners restructuring deal. College football faces a 30-day playoff expansion negotiation window with ESPN.
author: GoCheckMySports
key_fact: Wednesday brings institutional tests across sports: Judge's injury comeback will reveal his readiness for the Yankees' stretch run; the SEC's LSU vote Thursday will test whether a power conference can expel a flagship member; and LIV's bankruptcy filing marks the end of Saudi-funded golf as originally conceived, with player claims and tournament viability now court matters.
bottom_line: Judge returns to the Yankees Tuesday after three months of injury; the SEC votes Thursday on whether to expel LSU, marking a historic test of conference expulsion power; LIV Golf entered bankruptcy with BC Partners restructuring backing, leaving player claims and 2027 tournament viability as court matters; and the CFP opened a 30-day ESPN negotiation window on 24-team playoff expansion, with a December 1 decision deadline. The coming 72 hours will clarify whether major institutions can enforce accountability against their own members, and whether new governance models can emerge from insolvency.
body: Sports faced cascading institutional decisions and comebacks on Wednesday. Aaron Judge was activated off the 60-day injured list Monday and expected to play Tuesday against Colorado, ending a three-month absence from a right rib stress fracture sustained April 26. The Yankees went 45-39 without him after a 36-23 record with Judge; from June 1 through Sunday, the desk's league board shows the Yankees ranked 26th in the Majors in runs scored. Manager Aaron Boone indicated Judge might play five to seven innings initially and avoided diving to prevent re-injury. Judge declined a minor league rehab assignment, saying he did not see the point in wasting at-bats.

The SEC filed an amended federal complaint Tuesday seeking legal authority to expel LSU and scheduled a conference vote for Thursday, September 10. SEC bylaws require a two-thirds majority of presidents to approve expulsion. The filing adds LSU Board of Supervisors members and Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill as defendants and requests a temporary restraining order to prevent LSU from blocking the Thursday meeting. The dispute centers on LSU's recruitment of players with NFL contracts, including tight end Dae'Quan Wright and defensive lineman Zxavian Harris, both of whom the school did not roster for the season opener against Clemson. A Louisiana state court has already issued a preliminary injunction clearing the way for the players to compete, giving LSU legal grounds to contest SEC discipline and creating potential conflict between state and conference authority. In the SEC's 94-year history, no conference members have voted to expel another school; the only 21st-century precedent in a power conference came when the Big East expelled Temple following the 2004 season.

The filing estimates liabilities between $500 million and $1 billion against assets valued at $100 million to $500 million. The Saudi Public Investment Fund, which ended its funding in April 2026 after more than five years of investment, committed $49.6 million in debtor-in-possession financing to cover operations during restructuring. That covers less than 10 percent of estimated liabilities. The unsecured player creditors list includes at least $45 million in unpaid compensation, with Jon Rahm separately reported to be owed more than $100 million from his multiyear contract signed before the 2024 season. LIV's bankruptcy petition lists vendor IMG Media owed $3.2 million as the largest single amount among non-player creditors. The league intends to resume competition in 2027 under a player-majority ownership model with field sizes expanding to 75 players per event and Monday qualifiers introduced, though no definitive 2027 schedule has been announced. Contracts under the previous LIV iteration will terminate because of the court filing, and no obligation exists for players to sign with a restructured LIV 2.0 regardless of previous multi-year agreements.

The College Football Playoff triggered a 30-day negotiating window with ESPN on Tuesday, September 8, beginning formal discussions on expanding the playoff to 24 teams in 2027. The CFP's statement emphasized this does not represent a decision or commitment to expand but rather an opportunity to gather information. The window gives ESPN and the CFP until December 1 to reach agreement on revised media rights. On that same date, conferences must notify broadcast partners whether they intend to drop conference championship games, a procedural link tying format decisions to scheduling and media revenue.

Across tennis, Frances Tiafoe defeated Alex Michelsen 5-7, 3-6, 7-5, 6-3, 7-6 (10-6) in a US Open quarterfinal lasting 4 hours and 38 minutes on September 9, coming from two sets and a break down. The victory marked the first such comeback in a US Open men's quarterfinal since Roger Federer defeated Gael Monfils in 2014. Tiafoe will meet fellow American Tommy Shelton on Friday in the semifinal. In the women's draw on September 7, Zheng Qinwen defeated Iga Swiatek 7-5, 6-3, erasing a 5-0 first-set deficit. The comeback marks the second consecutive match in which Zheng has won seven games in a row from 0-5 down, against two Grand Slam champions, a pattern described as almost unheard of at the highest level.
